title: Electronegativity
short: Electronegativity measures how hard an atom pulls on shared electrons; it rises up and to the right.
trouble: Students give the noble gases the highest electronegativity, or confuse electronegativity with the number of valence electrons.

blocks.html: When two atoms share electrons in a bond, they do not always share evenly. One atom may pull the shared pair toward itself. That pull is electronegativity, and it follows the same pattern as Ionization Energy.

Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom attracts the electrons in a bond. It rises up and to the right on the periodic table. Fluorine is the most electronegative element (3.98 on the Pauling scale); cesium and francium are among the least. Most noble gases are left out because they rarely form bonds.

A bonding pair sits in the outer shells of both atoms. An atom with a large nuclear charge acting at a short distance (upper right) pulls that pair hard, exactly the conditions that make its ionization energy high. Linus Pauling built the scale from measured bond energies: bonds between atoms that differ a lot are extra strong, and the differences give each element a number. The values have no units; only differences between atoms matter.

blocks.title: Comparing two atoms
blocks.q: Which is more electronegative, oxygen or sulfur?
steps: They are in the same group; oxygen is one row higher.
Oxygen's outer electrons, and any bonding pair, are closer to its nucleus.
Oxygen (3.44) is more electronegative than sulfur (2.58).

blocks.title: Not the number of electrons
blocks.q: Oxygen has 6 valence electrons and chlorine has 7. Which is more electronegative?
steps: Oxygen is in period 2; chlorine is in period 3, one shell farther out.
The shorter distance wins: oxygen (3.44) beats chlorine (3.16).

blocks.html: Giving the noble gases the highest electronegativity (they have no ordinary bonds to measure), or treating electronegativity as the number of valence electrons. It is a pull, set by nuclear charge and distance. Check against fluorine: the closer an element is to fluorine on the table, the higher its value.
